result: The authors developed a frustrated Total Internal Reflection (fTIR) optical method coupled with high-speed imaging to track and quantify gait parameters in freely walking Drosophila with high temporal and spatial resolution. The method uses optical glass, LED light sources, and a high-speed camera recording at 250 fps with 4 ms temporal resolution and <4% optical distortion. Custom FlyWalker software automates footprint and body tracking.
evaluation: Claims C3, C25-C132 collectively describe the development and validation of the fTIR method. The technical specifications are clearly stated (C129-C130), optical distortion is measured (C132), and the physical principles are correctly described (C125-C128). The method is demonstrated with 71 videos (C28) and software is made freely available (C131). The approach is well-documented with figures and technical details.

result: Wild-type flies exhibit speed-dependent step parameters: average speeds ranged 7.2-44.7 mm/s with ~20 mm/s underrepresented; stance duration decreases with speed while swing duration remains constant; step period varies inversely with speed up to ~30 mm/s then plateaus at ~60 ms (16 Hz); step length and swing speed increase linearly with speed. Fast flies show metachronal lag equal to hindleg period (tripod gait), while slow flies show period-dependent lag (tetrapod gait).
evaluation: Claims C29-C40 describe comprehensive step parameter measurements supported by data in Figures 2B-F and statistical analyses. The observations are consistent with prior insect locomotion studies (C31 cites Wilson 1966, Graham 1972, Strauss & Heisenberg 1990). The distinction between tripod and tetrapod gaits based on metachronal lag (C35-C36) follows established definitions from Graham 1972. Sample size of 71 videos provides adequate statistical power.

result: Spatial parameters reveal that faster flies have straighter stance traces (lower stance linearity) that stabilize above ~34 mm/s, smaller footprint clustering values indicating more spatially restricted steps, and consistently smaller AEP clustering than PEP clustering (86% of videos). At faster speeds, AEP shifts anteriorly and PEP posteriorly for all legs; midlegs shift laterally while hindlegs position closer to the body.
evaluation: Claims C41-C50 describe spatial parameters supported by data in Figure 3. The stance linearity measurements (C41-C42) and footprint clustering analyses (C43-C47) are quantified with appropriate statistical tests. The AEP vs PEP difference (C45-C47) is robust across 86% of videos. The speed-dependent positional changes (C48-C50) are data-driven observations, though the functional interpretations (stability, power stroke) are speculative.

result: Flies preferentially use tripod gait but do not show abrupt gait transitions. Instead, the proportion of time in tripod vs tetrapod gait varies gradually with speed. Fast flies spend ~70% in tripod configuration, slow flies show highest tetrapod proportion. Noncanonical leg configurations account for 21-48% of combinations depending on speed, occurring primarily during gait transitions. Instantaneous speed shows wave-like patterns with peaks during stance phase and minima during transitions.
evaluation: Claims C51-C69 describe gait patterns supported by extensive data in Figure 4 and Table 1. The gradual rather than abrupt gait transitions (C62-C63) contrast with vertebrate locomotion and are well-documented. The quantification of tripod/tetrapod indexes (C59-C61, C65) and noncanonical combinations (C64, C66-C67) is thorough. The instantaneous speed analysis (C53-C56) is consistent with Graham 1972 observations in stick insects. Statistical tests confirm distinct gait indexes across speed groups (C59).

result: Footprint alignment analysis reveals a non-linear relationship with speed, with data clustering into three groups: large alignment values at slow speeds (<20 mm/s), small values at fast speeds (>34 mm/s), and no correlation at intermediate speeds. The transition at ~20 mm/s coincides with underrepresented speeds in the dataset, suggesting possible gait transitions. More aligned footprints in faster flies correlate with increased tripod index.
evaluation: Claims C70-C79 describe footprint alignment supported by Figure 5A-B. The follow-the-leader behavior (C70-C71) is well-established in hexapods with multiple citations. The non-linear relationship and three-group clustering (C73-C75) are clearly shown in Figure 5B with statistical significance. The correlation with tripod index (C77) supports functional interpretation. However, the inference about distinct motor circuits (C78) is speculative and would require additional experiments to confirm.

result: Contralateral legs within the same segment display average phase of ~0.5 in both slow and fast flies, consistent with coordinated walking. Slower animals show higher variability (shorter r vector). Phase values for ipsilateral adjacent legs decrease in slower animals, consistent with increased step period without proportional increase in step lag.
evaluation: Claims C80-C82 describe coordination parameters supported by radial plots in Figure 5C-E and supplementary figures. The phase value of ~0.5 for contralateral legs (C80) is expected for tripod gait and consistent with Graham 1972. The increased variability in slow flies (C81) and decreased ipsilateral phase values (C82) are data-driven observations with appropriate statistical analyses.

result: Inactivation of leg sensory neurons (nan36a mutant and 5-40Leg>TNT) led to deficient step precision including increased step length, wobbly body placement, larger footprint clustering variability, altered AEP/PEP, and increased swing/stance duration. However, interleg coordination, left-right coordination, and the ability to execute tripod gait were unaffected. Defects were more pronounced in slower flies. Control experiments with antenna removal confirmed phenotypes result from leg sensory feedback loss.
evaluation: Claims C4-C6 and C87-C124 describe sensory deprivation experiments supported by Figures 6-7 and Table 2. Two independent genetic approaches (nan mutant and TNT expression) show consistent phenotypes (C89-C104), strengthening conclusions. The preservation of tripod gait and coordination (C5-C6, C89-C90, C115) despite precision defects (C4, C91-C101) is surprising but well-documented. Antenna removal controls (C102) rule out confounding effects. Multiple regression analyses (Table 2) provide statistical rigor. The conclusion that proprioception is dispensable for coordination but required for precision (C124) is well-supported.

result: Several trends in sensory-deprived flies (AEP, PEP, footprint alignment, midleg positioning) resemble those in fast wild-type flies. Defects were more pronounced in slow sensory-deprived flies. These observations suggest flies use distinct neural programs at different speeds, with fast walking being less dependent on sensory feedback and relying more on CPG-interneuron communication, while slow walking invokes sensory feedback for complex terrain navigation.
evaluation: Claims C105-C108 and C120-C123 present an interpretive model based on comparisons between sensory-deprived and wild-type flies. While the observations (C105-C106, C103-C104, C120) are data-supported, the mechanistic interpretations about distinct neural programs (C107, C123), CPG-interneuron communication (C121), and speed-dependent sensory reliance (C108, C122) are speculative. These hypotheses are plausible and consistent with the data, but would require additional experiments (e.g., neural recordings, interneuron manipulations) to definitively establish the proposed mechanisms.

result: The fTIR apparatus can be used with other arthropods possessing adhesive tarsal structures, but the current setup cannot track individual leg joints, which is possible in larger insects like stick insects.
evaluation: Claims C110-C111 accurately describe the method's applicability and limitations. The requirement for adhesive structures (C110) is a physical constraint of the fTIR principle and is appropriately cited (Gorb et al. 2007). The limitation regarding joint tracking (C111) is an honest assessment of the method's spatial resolution compared to approaches used in larger insects (Cruse & Bartling 1995).

result: The authors discuss that their findings in Drosophila differ from stick insect studies where sensory feedback is required for interleg coordination. They speculate that when all six legs are equally impaired, flies resort to a CPG-interneuron dominated system sufficient for tripod gait execution, supported by observations that flies can recover partial tripod gait after single hindleg amputation.
evaluation: Claims C112-C119 present a discussion comparing results to prior work and proposing mechanisms. The stick insect literature (C112-C114) is accurately cited. However, the proposed mechanism involving CPG-interneuron communication (C116, C118) is speculative, acknowledged by the authors' use of "may be" and "we speculate." The supporting evidence from hindleg amputation studies (C119) is from other work (Wosnitza et al. 2012), not directly tested here. While the hypothesis is reasonable, it requires direct experimental validation.

result: The introduction establishes background knowledge about locomotion, CPGs, sensory feedback, and prior insect locomotion research, while identifying the gap in quantitative methods for analyzing Drosophila walking despite available genetic tools.
evaluation: Claims C1-C24 and C83-C86, C109 provide background context supported by appropriate citations to established literature. These claims accurately represent prior knowledge about locomotion principles (C1, C8-C13), insect studies (C14-C19), and the state of Drosophila research (C21-C24). The identification of the methodological gap (C22-C24) appropriately motivates the study. All background claims are properly attributed to cited sources.

result: Statistical analysis of the speed distribution shows it is not significantly different from normal (Shapiro-Wilk test, p=0.31), but normal probability plots reveal non-Gaussian outliers at <20 mm/s and >35 mm/s, suggesting the distribution has significant outliers in the tails.
evaluation: Claims C133-C134 describe statistical analyses of the speed distribution. The Shapiro-Wilk test result (C133) and normal probability plot interpretation (C134) are appropriate methods for assessing normality. The identification of non-Gaussian outliers at the speed ranges where other parameters show transitions is consistent with the overall findings about potential gait transitions at these speeds.
